source_title: 2022 ACC Expert Consensus Decision Pathway on the Evaluation and Disposition of Acute Chest Pain in the Emergency Department
locator: Sections 5.2.1 (Initial ECG Interpretation), 5.3 (hs-cTn Assays), and pathway figures; key points 1–3
source_setting: U.S. emergency department; adult acute chest-pain evaluation, especially possible ACS; requires validated high-sensitivity troponin assay pathways.
value: Obtain and interpret an ECG within 10 minutes of ED arrival; review prehospital ECG when available.
Patients with ischemic ECG findings follow acute STEMI/NSTE-ACS guidance; nonischemic ECG patients may enter an accelerated clinical decision pathway.
Use assay-specific high-sensitivity troponin testing and serial change within a validated rapid pathway to guide rule-out, observation/testing, or high-risk disposition.
source_evidence_basis: The consensus pathway states ECG should be obtained/interpreted within 10 minutes, identifies ischemic ECG as prompting acute ACS guideline management, and describes hs-cTn rapid pathways for patients with nonischemic ECGs. The source specifically cautions these pathways are not suitable for older-generation assays.
limitations: Clinical pathway, not a complete differential for all chest pain. Depends on local validated assay-specific thresholds and timing; definite ACS management is outside this document’s scope.
inferred_scenario_use: A synthetic ED case may expose arrival, ECG interpretation, troponin collection/result review, risk-pathway branch, and disposition as separate decisions; do not simulate numeric assay thresholds without local validated protocol and clinician review.
applicability: Adult ED patients with acute chest pain and possible ACS; not an automatic diagnosis or treatment rule.
source_period: 2022 consensus pathway (publication date 2022-10-11); no cohort period applies.
source_n: Not applicable; guideline/pathway, not a patient cohort
role_assignment_basis: Role participants are proposed scenario assignments inferred from the pathway setting for simulation design; the cited source does not enumerate this exact role list.

source_title: ACR Appropriateness Criteria®: Acute Hand and Wrist Trauma
locator: Variant 1: Suspect acute hand or wrist trauma, initial imaging; Variant 2: initial radiographs negative or equivocal, next imaging study; narrative pages 3–5
source_setting: Acute hand/wrist trauma imaging decision support; suspected adult wrist fracture case is within scope, though recommendations cover broader ages and hand injuries.
value: For suspected acute hand/wrist trauma, initial radiographs of the area of interest are usually appropriate.

If initial radiographs are negative or equivocal but clinical suspicion persists, ACR lists repeat radiographs in 10–14 days, noncontrast CT, or noncontrast MRI as usually appropriate next imaging options.
source_evidence_basis: The ACR Appropriateness Criteria narrative’s Variant 1 rates radiography as usually appropriate for suspected acute hand/wrist trauma. Variant 2 lists repeat radiographs, CT without IV contrast, and MRI without IV contrast as usually appropriate after negative/equivocal radiographs.
limitations: Imaging appropriateness guidance does not determine individual immobilization, reduction, referral, or discharge; the repeat-radiograph option may delay diagnosis. Do not infer fracture absence from a negative initial study when suspicion remains.
inferred_scenario_use: Model initial assessment and radiographs, then branch by result and continuing clinician suspicion to follow-up imaging or other locally approved care.
applicability: Acute trauma with suspected wrist/hand injury; adapt to patient age, examination, pregnancy status, and local imaging/referral pathways.
source_period: ACR narrative identifies the topic as revised in 2018; whether superseded or reaffirmed is not stated on the accessed narrative (retrieved 2026-10-10).
source_n: Not applicable; guideline/pathway, not a patient cohort

source_title: 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
locator: Section 2.7 Emergency Evaluation of Patients With Suspected Stroke; Section 3.2 Initial, Vascular, and Multimodal Imaging Approaches; Figure 2
source_setting: Acute hospital and prehospital stroke systems; primarily adult suspected acute ischemic stroke, with specified pediatric recommendations.
value: Activate the local suspected-stroke/ED-stroke-team process and establish the clinical timeline, including last-known-well, during initial evaluation.

Obtain emergent brain imaging (noncontrast CT or MRI) to assess ischemic burden and exclude intracranial hemorrhage before reperfusion intervention. AHA/ASA calls for imaging as rapidly as possible (example: within 25 minutes); its supporting text says door-to-imaging times of 25 minutes or less have been achieved in some settings and MRI-first hospitals should strive for similar times.
When suspected large-vessel occlusion warrants vascular imaging, do not delay emergent CTA/CTP to obtain serum creatinine.
source_evidence_basis: The 2026 AHA/ASA guideline §§2.7 and 3.2 address ED/stroke-team evaluation and imaging. Recommendation 2 in §3.2 says systems should use process-improvement protocols for imaging as rapidly as possible (e.g., within 25 minutes). Supporting text explains door-to-imaging times ≤25 minutes have been achieved in various settings and MRI-first hospitals should strive for comparable times; this is an example/process aim, not a universal guaranteed threshold.
limitations: The guideline’s recommendations require clinical eligibility assessment and local stroke protocols; the within-25-minute language is an example/process aim supported by observed feasibility in some settings, not a universal guaranteed patient-level threshold. Avoid encoding treatment eligibility from isolated time or imaging fields.
inferred_scenario_use: Use a witnessed-onset or uncertain-onset synthetic case to teach timeline capture, stroke-team activation, imaging choice, and specialist disposition decisions; clinician adjudication is needed for interpretation and treatment selection.
applicability: Suspected acute stroke pathway; adult AIS guidance, with separate pediatric provisions. Hemorrhagic stroke and stroke mimics remain in the diagnostic differential.
source_period: Originally published 2026-01-26; guideline literature review searched through March 2025 with later high-impact publications added where appropriate.
source_n: Not applicable; guideline/pathway, not a patient cohort

source_title: Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention, 2026 Update
locator: Chapter 9, Emergency Department Management of Exacerbations (Adults, Adolescents, Children 6–11 years), pp. 184–186; Chapter 12, children 5 years and younger, Box 12-3, p. 219.
source_setting: Acute-care/emergency assessment; GINA distinguishes children 6–11 years and children 5 years and younger.
value: Take a brief history and perform examination concurrently with prompt therapy; assess severity, vital signs/oxygen saturation, response to treatment, risk factors, and alternative or additional causes of breathlessness.
For children under 18, consider a validated assessment tool such as PRAM; monitor oxygen saturation and, where feasible without delaying care, lung function before treatment and during response.

For children 5 and younger, features such as inability to speak/drink, cyanosis, respiratory rate above 40/min, room-air oxygen saturation below 92%, or quiet chest are immediate hospital-transfer indicators in the GINA box.
source_evidence_basis: GINA 2026 text under ED management specifies concurrent brief history/physical exam and prompt therapy, severity/vital-sign assessment, differential causes, objective assessment, and PRAM consideration for under-18s. Box 12-3 provides the listed under-5 transfer indicators.
limitations: The under-5 transfer signs are age-specific and must not be generalized to older children. This record deliberately omits treatment doses; GINA itself notes oximetry limitations including potential overestimation in people with dark skin and altitude adjustments.
inferred_scenario_use: Use age-banded cases to represent assessment, escalation, response reassessment, and disposition; do not turn the guideline into an autonomous treatment order.
applicability: Pediatric acute asthma exacerbation assessment in acute care; distinguish age bands and assess competing diagnoses.
source_period: 2026 Strategy Report; GINA announced the report in May 2026. No patient cohort period applies.
source_n: Not applicable; guideline/pathway, not a patient cohort

source_title: Hospital-Based Triage of Obstetric Patients, Committee Opinion No. 667
source_setting: Hospital-based obstetric triage; pregnant patients presenting for urgent assessment, including coordination between obstetric units and EDs.
value: Establish hospital-specific triage guidelines collaboratively among obstetric units, emergency departments, ancillary services, and external emergency-response systems.
Use a validated obstetric triage acuity tool as a candidate template to guide prompt evaluation and resource use, adapted to the individual hospital unit.
source_evidence_basis: ACOG Committee Opinion 667 explicitly recommends collaboration across obstetric units, EDs, ancillary services, and outside emergency response systems; it says recently developed validated acuity tools may guide quality, efficiency, and resource use and serve as templates for individual units.
limitations: This is a systems-level recommendation, not a universal acuity algorithm or fixed timing rule. ACOG states its guidance is not an exclusive course of care and may change; verify current local protocol and current ACOG status before clinical use.
inferred_scenario_use: A synthetic triage scenario can model pregnancy-related presentation, acuity assessment, maternal/fetal considerations, and routing among ED, obstetric unit, and ancillary services as locally configured decisions.
applicability: Hospital-based triage of obstetric patients; local facility determines location, staffing, timing, and validated acuity tool.
source_period: Committee Opinion No. 667, issued July 2016; current reaffirmation/update status is not established by the accessed page (retrieved 2026-10-10).
source_n: Not applicable; guideline/pathway, not a patient cohort

source_title: 2025 National Guidelines for a Behavioral Health Coordinated System of Crisis Care
locator: Executive Summary / “Essential Elements of a Crisis System”; system elements “Someone to Contact,” “Someone to Respond,” and “A Safe Place for Help”
source_setting: U.S. community behavioral-health crisis systems, including crisis lines, mobile crisis response, and stabilization settings; not an ED-specific clinical decision algorithm.
value: Connect people in crisis to immediate contact support (e.g., 988 or another behavioral-health hotline).
Dispatch mobile crisis response based on assessed need, with de-escalation and connection to care.
Route to an appropriate safe stabilization setting for immediate treatment/support, with crisis-system coordination.
source_evidence_basis: SAMHSA 2025 national guidance names three foundational system elements: someone to contact, someone to respond, and a safe place for help; it describes hotline/988, mobile crisis teams, and stabilization services respectively.
limitations: Community system design guidance, not a patient-level suicide-risk assessment, involuntary-hold rule, or ED disposition protocol. Actual service availability and escalation criteria vary by jurisdiction.
inferred_scenario_use: Represent crisis presentation as a safety and needs assessment followed by locally available contact/response/stabilization options; urgent medical needs and immediate safety concerns require human clinician judgment and local emergency procedures.
applicability: Behavioral-health emergency/crisis system planning in the U.S.; local service map and legal requirements determine operational routing.
source_period: 2025 national guideline; SAMHSA resource page lists publication date 2025-01-15. No patient cohort period applies.
source_n: Not applicable; guideline/pathway, not a patient cohort
